issues.legal_issue: Rights claimed under an unregistered instrument that required registration could not be entertained.
material_facts: Some claims rested on unregistered instruments purporting to grant rights to collect forest produce.
The claimed rights were treated as potentially conveying an interest in proprietary rights or a profit à prendre, rather than merely recording a bare licence.
issues.conclusion: The claims based on the unregistered instruments could not be entertained.
issues.legal_principle: Under Shrimathi Shantabai v. State of Bombay, an instrument conveying a part or share in proprietary rights, or a profit à prendre, requires registration; without registration, the claimed rights cannot be established on the instrument.

predicates.article_32_petition: The claimant brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.unregistered_instrument: The instrument on which the claimant relied was not registered.
predicates.instrument_claims_transfer_of_registrabl: The claimant relied on an instrument that purported to convey a proprietary interest or a right to take produce from land.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petition relies on an unregistered instrument purporting to transfer a registrable right, the claim based on that instrument cannot be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A writ cannot enforce an agreement after its stipulated period has expired.
material_facts: Some agreements had expired before the petitions were decided.
The claimants sought relief by constitutional petitions to enforce rights under those agreements.
issues.conclusion: No writ could issue to enforce the expired agreements; any remedy, if available, was an action for breach of contract.
issues.legal_principle: An expired agreement leaves no subsisting contractual right for a writ to enforce; any remedy for its breach lies in a suit. The Court applied this principle to the constitutional petitions before it.

predicates.article_32_petition: The claimant brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.agreement_period_expired: The period during which the agreement operated had ended before the claimant sought enforcement.

issues.definition: If a claimant seeks enforcement through a constitutional petition after the agreement has expired, a writ is unavailable to enforce that agreement.

issues.legal_issue: Agreements granting long-term rights to forest produce together with ancillary rights to use land are not contracts for the sale of goods simpliciter.
material_facts: The agreements granted rights over periods extending beyond the immediate collection of leaves.
They covered forest produce beyond tendu leaves, including timber and bamboos, and included rights to prune, coppice and burn trees.
They also permitted the use and occupation of land, construction of storage buildings, and manufacture of bricks for the business.
issues.conclusion: The agreements could not be characterized as contracts for the sale of goods simpliciter.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the definitions of goods and immovable property in the General Clauses Act, the Sale of Goods Act, the Transfer of Property Act and the Registration Act. Because the agreements conveyed rights beyond the collection of leaves, including rights relating to trees, other forest produce and land, they were not merely sales of goods. The Court distinguished the reasoning in Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel and Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and considered the principle in Mohanlal Hargovind of Jubbalpore v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Central Provinces and Berar.

predicates.agreement_grants_long_term_forest_produc: The grant gives the recipient rights over forest produce for an extended period, rather than only an immediate purchase of existing produce.
predicates.agreement_includes_ancillary_land_or_tre: The grant also permits use of land or activities involving trees, buildings, or other forest resources.

issues.definition: An agreement granting extended forest-produce rights together with ancillary rights to use land or trees is not merely a sale of goods.

issues.legal_issue: Proprietary rights in forests and trees conveyed through a proprietor vest in the State when the statutory abolition of those proprietary rights takes effect.
material_facts: The statutory scheme treated forests and trees within an estate as items of proprietary rights belonging to the proprietors.
The agreements conveyed rights to forest produce and associated rights over the land and trees to the claimants.
The claimants challenged the State's action after the statutory vesting of proprietary rights.
issues.conclusion: The rights conveyed under the agreements were proprietary rights and vested in the State under sections 3 and 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 provide for proprietary rights, including the rights and interests of persons claiming through the proprietor, to vest in the State. The Court read these provisions with sections 2(13) and 47(3) and section 202 of the Central Provinces Land Revenue Act, 1917, which supported the conclusion that forests and trees belonged to proprietors as items of proprietary rights. The Court did not follow Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel and Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, treating its characterization of the grants as bare licences as per incuriam.

predicates.statutory_vesting_challenge: The claimant challenges the consequences of a statutory process that transfers proprietary rights in an estate to the State.
predicates.forest_or_tree_rights_belong_to_propriet: The forest or tree rights at issue form part of proprietary rights held by the proprietor of the estate.
predicates.agreement_transfers_proprietary_forest_r: The agreement conveys those proprietary forest or tree rights, or an interest in them, from the proprietor to another person.

issues.definition: When a statutory vesting challenge concerns forest or tree rights belonging to a proprietor and an agreement transferred those proprietary rights, the transferred rights vest in the State.

issues.legal_issue: A State's refusal to be bound by a private contract or licence does not infringe a fundamental right when the State has not acquired or taken possession of that contract or licence.
material_facts: The claimants argued that the State had to honor agreements made by former proprietors.

The Court held that, if the agreements created only contractual rights or licences rather than proprietary rights, the State had not acquired or taken possession of those rights under the abolition legislation.
The petitions sought enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 32.
issues.conclusion: If the agreements created only contractual rights or licences, the State's refusal to be bound by them did not infringe a fundamental right supporting relief under Article 32.
issues.legal_principle: Under Ananda Behera v. State of Orissa and Shrimathi Shantabai v. State of Bombay, a State that does not acquire or take possession of a private contract or licence, but merely declines to be bound by it, has not thereby infringed a fundamental right. A licence also comes to an end with the extinction of the licensor's title.

predicates.article_32_petition: The claimant brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.claimant_right_is_only_contractual_or_li: The claimant's entitlement is only a personal contractual right or licence, not a proprietary right in the land or its resources.
predicates.state_did_not_acquire_or_take_possession: The State did not take possession of or acquire the claimant's contract or licence, but declined to be bound by it.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petitioner has only a contractual or licence-based entitlement and the State has not acquired or taken possession of it, there is no fundamental-right infringement supporting relief in the petition.
